In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix buffer overflow in SMB2_tcon()

In SMB2_tcon(), unc_path is allocated with a fixed buffer size of
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH * 2 bytes (672 bytes). However, the user-controlled
UNC path (tree) length is passed to cifs_strtoUTF16(), which assumes the
destination buffer is large enough and writes strlen(tree) + 1 UTF-16 code
units.

Commit 62a1a439e0fd ("cifs: clean up handling of unc= option") removed the
length check on UNC mount options, allowing mount paths to exceed
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH while retaining the fixed-size buffer allocation in
SMB2_tcon(). Consequently, an oversized UNC string causes cifs_strtoUTF16()
to write past the end of the heap object, resulting in a slab-out-of-bounds
write. Furthermore, if a tree exceeds MAX_TREE_SIZE characters, strscpy()
truncates it in cifs_tcon::tree_name, causing subsequent reconnects or
failovers to fail.

Fix this by first verifying that the length of tree does not exceed
MAX_TREE_SIZE, returning -EINVAL if it does. Then, dynamically allocate
unc_path based on the length of tree so that it safely accommodates all
UTF-16 code units for paths within MAX_TREE_SIZE.

[pc: remove unused MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: don't resurrect an exiting tcon from cached dir workers

cfids_laundromat_worker() bumps tcon->tc_count for every expired open
cfid and queues cached_dir_offload_close() without checking whether the
tcon is already being torn down.  Racing with the final cifs_put_tcon(),
the tcon comes back from zero and gets torn down twice:

  T1                                  T2
  cifs_put_tcon()
   --tc_count == 0, TID_EXITING
   tconInfoFree()
    free_cached_dirs()
     cancel_delayed_work_sync()       cfids_laundromat_worker()
                                       ++tc_count == 1
                                       queue_work(serverclose_wq)
    kfree(tcon->origin_fullpath)
    kfree(tcon)
                                      cached_dir_offload_close()
                                       close_cached_dir()  [UAF]
                                       cifs_put_tcon()
                                        tconInfoFree()     [double free]

cached_dir_lease_break() also bumps tc_count without tc_lock, racing with
the laundromat's locked update.

Take the tcon reference through a helper that refuses once the tcon is
TID_EXITING or its refcount has dropped to zero.  Queued put_work and
close_work then always hold a tcon reference, so tconInfoFree() can't
run before they finish and free_cached_dirs() doesn't need to flush any
workqueue.  If the laundromat can't get a reference, put the cfid back on
the dying list for free_cached_dirs() to free; its handle goes away with
the tree connection.

The lease break path finds the tcon on ses->tcon_list under
cifs_tcp_ses_lock, so it can't see TID_EXITING, but it now takes tc_lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: bound POSIX lock data area by response length

CIFSSMBPosixLock() receives a TRANS2 response whose server-provided
DataOffset and DataCount are not required by validate_t2() to describe an
interval inside the response. A server can therefore make the client read a
cifs_posix_lock beyond the response buffer and return those kernel bytes
through F_GETLK.

Use smbCalcSize() to obtain the full response length after any multipart
TRANS2 reassembly, then reject data areas that extend past it before
dereferencing them.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: fix buffer length underflow in RDMA transfers

When a remote buffer descriptor is larger than the remaining local
buffer, smbdirect_connection_rdma_xmit() clamps its length and sets
buf_len to zero. The common accounting code then subtracts the clamped
length from buf_len, causing it to underflow. If another descriptor
follows, the loop processes it with a wrapped remaining length and
includes memory beyond the local buffer in the RDMA transfer.

A client can trigger an out-of-bounds kernel write with an SMB WRITE
request, or an out-of-bounds kernel read with an SMB READ request, by
supplying multiple RDMA buffer descriptors with an oversized descriptor
before the last one.

Remove the premature assignment to buf_len. Subtracting the clamped length
already consumes the remaining buffer, so the next iteration stops and
only descriptors within the local buffer are used to build work requests.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: server: size directory name conversion buffer correctly

A 2048-byte ASCII directory name needs 4098 bytes when converted to
UTF-16, including the terminator. ksmbd_convert_dir_info_name() caps
its allocation at PATH_MAX and writes past the end of that buffer.

Allocate space for one UTF-16 code unit per input byte plus the
terminator. Use kmalloc_array() to check the size calculation.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: fix correction of unwritten extents in quota file data fork

LOLLM noticed a couple of problems with the code that fixes unwritten
mappings in the quota file's data fork: first, we should zero the ondisk
contents as part of converting them to "unwritten" just in case we crash
shortly after the conversion.  Second, and more importantly, it noticed
that we fail to resynchronize the iext tree cursor after modifying the
iext tree.  If the tree shape changes, we could be in a world of hurt.
Third, we should force a quotacheck if we reset an ondisk dquot.  Fix
all issues.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: don't try to scrub self-referential dirent in metapath checker

LOLLM observes that the _ilock_both helper will loop forever trying to
double-lock the same inode if mpath->dp == sc->ip.  Callers are not
supposed to call us with parent == child because that makes no sense.
Trigger an assertion, mark the scan incomplete, and return IO error
so that this fails noisily.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: don't subtract excess usage twice when computing agf_btreeblks

LOLLM noticed that the free space btree repair code calculates
agf_btreeblks from the number of blocks we wrote to rebuild the free
space btrees (minus the roots).  That's correct.  However, it observes
that we subtract the "excess" reservation, which is not correct.  Fix
this accounting problem.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: don't overrun incore inode when cleaning attr forks

LOLLM noticed that xrep_dinode_check_afork doesn't check for a
di_forkoff value that is so large that the attr fork would begin after
the end of the inode space.  This causes afork_{ptr,size} to be
nonsense.  What we really ought to do here is zap the attr fork.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: complain loudly when dirtree checker finds broken links

LOLLM observed that the directory tree walk code bails out if it finds
broken parent pointers along the way.  However, it flattens the return
code to zero, which means that we can end up in the repair code having
not completed the scan.  We should never proceed with a repair in this
state, so let's mark the scrub incomplete and exit.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: bound inode fork length against the fork size during log recovery

xlog_recover_inode_commit_pass2() copies an inode log item's data/attr
fork region into the inode buffer using the on-log region length without
bounding it against the fork capacity, e.g.:

	len = item->ri_buf[2].iov_len;
	memcpy(XFS_DFORK_DPTR(dip), src, len);

The only guard is an ASSERT, which is a no-op on production kernels
(CONFIG_XFS_DEBUG off), and xfs_dinode_verify() runs only after the copy.
A crafted image with a dirty log can therefore drive a heap out-of-bounds
write at mount time. The XFS_ILOG_DBROOT sibling already passes
XFS_DFORK_DSIZE as a bound; the DDATA/DEXT and ADATA/AEXT memcpy paths
did not.

Bound each logged fork region against the destination fork size before
copying it, and reject the log item with -EFSCORRUPTED when it does not
fit. Because the recovered inode is only verified after the fork data has
been copied in, the checks are done up front, before any memcpy into the
on-disk inode.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: bound da-node entry count against the correct geometry

xfs_da3_node_verify() bounds the node entry count against the larger of
the directory and attribute geometries because, as a buffer verifier, it
cannot tell whether the block belongs to the directory or the attribute
tree. When the directory block size exceeds the fs block size (e.g.
mkfs.xfs -n size=64k -b size=4k), an attribute node buffer is a single fs
block that holds only m_attr_geo->node_ents entries, yet a crafted attr
node may claim a count up to m_dir_geo->node_ents and still pass the
verifier.

xfs_da3_node_lookup_int() then indexes btree[] up to that count during
its binary search -- an out-of-bounds read via getxattr/listxattr on a
mounted crafted image.

The buffer verifier is the wrong place to tighten this: it has no fork
context, and the transaction-less read path used by getxattr does not run
xfs_da3_node_set_type() either. xfs_da3_node_lookup_int(), on the other
hand, always runs on that path and holds args->geo, the geometry of the
fork actually being searched. Bound the entry count against
args->geo->node_ents there, before walking the entries.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: always report inode repair setup failures

LOLLM noticed that xchk_setup_inode silently discards errors being
returned by xrep_setup_inode.  Fix that, and fix the stub macro so that

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: always forget cached ACLs if the attr fork swap succeeds

LOLLM complains that xrep_xattr_rebuild_tree omits the xfs_forget_acl
call if the attr fork swap succeeds (and hence the acls might have
changed) but reaping the old attr fork fails.  Fix it so that we always
purge the cached acls if the swap succeeds, even if subsequent steps do
not.  This avoids some cache coherency problems with access controls.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: reject remote xattr entries with an out-of-range value length

xfs_attr3_leaf_verify_entry() validates a remote attribute entry's name
but never bounds its on-disk value length (xfs_attr_leaf_name_remote.
valuelen, a __be32). A crafted leaf with valuelen = 0x80000000 passes
the verifier and the CRC.

That length is later assigned into the signed int args->rmtvaluelen
(xfs_attr3_leaf_getvalue), becoming negative, which slips past the signed
-ERANGE check in xfs_attr_copy_value(); a getxattr() with a small buffer
then memcpy()s a full remote block into the small kvalue buffer
(xfs_attr_rmtval_copyout) -- a heap out-of-bounds write with
attacker-controlled content, from an unprivileged getxattr(2) on a
mounted crafted image.

Reject remote entries whose value length exceeds XFS_XATTR_SIZE_MAX in
the leaf verifier, so the malicious block is rejected at read time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: reject out-of-range attribute value lengths in xfs_attr_copy_value

xfs_attr_copy_value() takes the value length as a signed int and, for a
remote xattr, is handed args->rmtvaluelen.  That field is filled from the
on-disk __be32 xfs_attr_leaf_name_remote.valuelen in
xfs_attr3_leaf_getvalue(), so a crafted length such as 0x80000000 is
stored into the signed rmtvaluelen as a negative number.

The "buffer too small" guard in xfs_attr_copy_value() is a signed
comparison:

	if (args->valuelen < valuelen)
		return -ERANGE;

A negative valuelen therefore compares as smaller than the caller's
buffer size, skips the -ERANGE path, and is then used as a copy length,
leading to an out-of-bounds copy of a full remote block into a small
getxattr(2) buffer on a mounted crafted image.

Reject a value length that is negative or larger than the maximum xattr
size before it is used, so a bogus on-disk length can no longer slip
through the value copier.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rtnetlink: wait for RCU readers in rtnl_link_unregister()

rtnl_link_ops_get() finds ops on link_ops under rcu_read_lock() and only
then takes ops->srcu. rtnl_link_unregister() unlinks ops, then calls
synchronize_srcu() and cleanup_srcu_struct() without first waiting for
RCU readers. A reader that found ops before list_del_rcu() and has not yet
taken ops->srcu is not waited for.

Such a reader then locks a cleaned-up srcu_struct and keeps using ops
after the module that owns it is gone. rtnl_newlink() and
rtnl_dump_ifinfo() both look up ops without RTNL, the latter for any
user that dumps links filtered by kind.

With delays added between the lookup and srcu_read_lock() in
rtnl_link_ops_get(), and before rtnl_link_ops_put() in
rtnl_dump_ifinfo(), running "ip link show type dummy" alongside
"rmmod dummy" on a KASAN kernel gives:

  BUG: KASAN: vmalloc-out-of-bounds in __srcu_read_unlock+0x57/0x70
  Read of size 8 at addr ffffffffc02ff318 by task ip/147
  Call Trace:
   __srcu_read_unlock+0x57/0x70
   rtnl_dump_ifinfo.cold+0x30/0x3b
   rtnl_dumpit+0x7a/0x1b0
   netlink_dump+0x486/0x11b0
   __netlink_dump_start+0x661/0x910
   rtnetlink_rcv_msg+0x611/0x9e0
   netlink_rcv_skb+0x126/0x380
   netlink_unicast+0x605/0x830
   netlink_sendmsg+0x6d0/0xbb0
   __sys_sendto+0x335/0x3a0

Call synchronize_rcu() before synchronize_srcu(), as
rtnl_af_unregister() already does. This should be enough because
rtnl_link_ops_get() is the only RCU walker of link_ops, and it takes
ops->srcu before rcu_read_unlock(), so every reader that found ops is
covered by synchronize_srcu() once the RCU grace period ends. The extra
grace period only costs time at module unload.

Readers and the writer were serialized by RTNL until link_ops got its
own mutex, which is why the missing RCU wait did not matter before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: nft_payload: restrict checksum offsets to known values

We need to prevent userspace from corrupting e.g. tcp->doff, because
many locations in conntrack and conntrack helpers rely on
nf_conntrack_in() having validated the packet headers.
nft_payload allows to alter headers later which invalidates this
assumption.

The 'Fixes' commit restricts writes to safe fields, but there is
another side channel: the checksum location.

Restrict this too.  Reported via sashiko/gemini.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: mark overfull dabtree node blocks as corrupt

LOLLM observes that we need to range-check the dabtree node record count
before using it to index an array.  Fix that.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: check fork type against dabtree block magic number

LOLLM complains that we fail to flag dabtree blocks that should never be
associated with the file fork -- data forks can't point to xattr leaves,
and attr forks can't point to dirent blocks.  Add the missing checks.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: abort dirtree repair if the live update hook dies

LOLLM notices that if the live update hook for the directory tree repair
code hits an error, it will set dl->aborted and stops working.  If the
repair code ever sees that condition, it ought to bail out immediately
instead of continuing with obsolete data.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: fix lost errno returned from xfarray_foliosort

LOLLM noticed that we stop the sort early but don't actually pass along
the error code, which could enable repair code to continue running with
an unsorted array.  Fix that.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: don't repair fs summary counters with garbage

LOLLM noticed that if we scan the filesystem and come up with totally
garbage numbers for the summary counters, we don't actually mark the
scan incomplete.  Because we don't do this, repair can install the
garbage values into the filesystem, making things worse.  Don't do that.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: don't proceed with xattr repair if the live update fails

LOLLM observes that we ought to make one last check for failed live
updates before replacing the xattr structure.  Let's be cautious here.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: don't fix the directory tree if live update fails

LOLLM complains that we don't double-check dl->aborted one last time to
before committing repairs to the filesystem.  This is important because
the live update handler could have set ->aborted if it encountered a
runtime error.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: always reset incore attr fork buffer when resetting fork

LOLLM noticed that the local format attr fork verifier depends on
if_bytes being set correctly.  However, the fork reset function doesn't
reset that correctly, which can cause post-repair verifier failures.
Fix that.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: actually lock the metafile reservation when adjusting after repair

LOLLM reported that xrep_reset_metafile_resv performs unlocked loads
and stores to the metadata file space reservation counters and thus can
race with other threads.  Fix this by taking the lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: avoid cross-rtgroup reaping after a repair

LOLLM notices that the extents stored in a xrtb_bitmap (aka xfs_rtblock
bitmap) can span multiple rtgroups due to two circumstances.  The first
is that the size of an rtgroup is an exact power of two, which means
that rtgroups are adjacent in the segmented xfs_rtblock_t address space.
This is fairly common to reduce the amount of multiplication and
division needed to handle space on the rt volume.

The second is that (unlike in the original rtgroups design), rtgroups do
not have fixed-location metadata like AGs do, which means that there's
nothing to force a break between rtgroups.

Therefore, we must loop through the rtgroups in xreap_rtmeta_extent to
avoid running off the end of an rtgroup while reaping.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: fix buffer overruns in xfs_ioc_attr_list

When we converted the al_offset array in struct xfs_attrlist into a VLA,
the size of the object shrank by 4 bytes.  Unfortunately, the buffer
size validation in the attrlist ioctl wasn't updated to notice this, so
the al_offset[0] assignment blindly writes off the end of the buffer.
LOLLM noticed the omitted check and complained.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: skip copy up of empty security.capability

ovl_copy_xattr() gives up if it can't read an attribute that
listxattr() has named.  An empty security.capability, which anybody has
been able to store on any file for a long time, is such a case: it is
listed, and getxattr() has nothing to return for it.  A file in a lower
layer that carries one can't be copied up: it can't be written to,
renamed or have its mode changed.

There is nothing to copy if there are no data.  Go on with the next
one.

[amir: treat -EINVAL as no capability too, and do the same in
 ovl_copy_up_meta_inode_data()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: set the revalidate flags after d_instantiate()

stat() of a file on an overlayfs mount triggers a kernel warning and
fails with ECHILD if another task is creating that file at the same
time. This happens on an overlay with a FUSE upper layer, which is the
layer where overlayfs creates new files. Write access to a directory on
such an overlay is all a user needs to run the two tasks.

The revalidate flags are DCACHE_OP_REVALIDATE and
DCACHE_OP_WEAK_REVALIDATE. They tell path walk to call ->d_revalidate()
or ->d_weak_revalidate() on a dentry, so that the filesystem can check
that the cached dentry is still valid. An overlay dentry only has one of
these flags if a dentry in one of its layers has it. FUSE dentries have
the first one.

When a flag is set on an overlay dentry, path walk calls
ovl_dentry_revalidate_common(). That function only expects a dentry
without an inode in RCU walk, while the dentry is being destroyed. For
such a dentry outside of RCU walk, it hits a WARN_ON() and
returns -ECHILD. So a negative overlay dentry must never have the flags
set.

ovl_instantiate() breaks this rule. When a task creates a file, the
overlay dentry for the new name is hashed but still negative.
ovl_instantiate() then works in this order:

- It copies the flags from the new upper dentry to the overlay dentry.
- It calls ovl_get_inode(), which can sleep in a getxattr request to the
  FUSE server.
- Only then does it call d_instantiate().

A second task that looks up the name between the first step and the last
finds a negative dentry with the flags set and revalidates it.

Reproduced with a FUSE server that delays its getxattr reply: stat() of
a name that was being created hit the WARN_ON() and failed with ECHILD.

Fix this by setting the flags after d_instantiate().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: read the nlink xattr of every indexed non-dir

With nfs_export=on, data written through a file handle to a lower file,
i.e. a file that exists only in a lower layer of the overlay, can be
lost on the next mount. A lookup of the file by name then returns -EIO.
Also, a file with one name reports st_nlink 2 once it has been copied to
the upper layer. After such a file is removed, its file handle can still
open it until the next mount.

Before a lower file is changed for the first time, overlayfs copies it
to the writable upper layer. This is called copy up.

The index directory is $workdir/index, where $workdir is the directory
given by the workdir= option. Each entry is named after the file handle
of a lower inode, so that overlayfs can get from the handle to the
copied up inode.

With nfs_export=on, copy up indexes every non-directory: it copies the
file to an entry in the index directory and then hard links that entry
into the upper directory. The index entry is an extra link to the upper
inode, so overlayfs stores the link count that users should see in the
overlay.nlink xattr.

A file can also be opened by handle, either by an NFS client or by a
process with CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH calling open_by_handle_at(). If the
file is not in the dcache, its overlay dentry is disconnected, i.e. it
has no parent yet. Copy up then creates the index entry but no hard link
in the upper directory. The index entry has i_nlink 1 and holds the only
copy of the data written to the file.

ovl_get_nlink() reads the stored count. Its caller passes a default,
which the function returns if there is no stored count. If the lower
inode has i_nlink 1, the function returns the default without reading
the xattr. That was correct as long as only lower files with multiple
links were indexed.

On the next mount, ovl_verify_index() looks for orphans, i.e. index
entries of files whose last name was removed. For an index entry with
i_nlink 1, it passes a default of 0 to ovl_get_nlink() and treats a
result of 0 as an orphan. Here the lower inode also has i_nlink 1, so
the result is the default. ovl_indexdir_cleanup() then replaces the
entry with a whiteout, which in the index marks a file as deleted. The
written data is lost.

A lookup by name then returns -EIO, because a whiteout as the index
entry of a lower file that still exists is a bad index.

ovl_get_inode() gets the wrong count the same way. Its default is the
i_nlink of the upper inode, which includes the index entry, so a copied
up file with one name reports st_nlink 2.

When that name is removed, the count drops to 1 rather than 0.
ovl_nlink_end() replaces the index entry with a whiteout only at a count
of 0, so the entry stays, and the handle of the removed file still opens
it.

Reproduced by writing through open_by_handle_at() to an uncached lower
file with one link. After a remount the data was lost, and the name
returned EIO.

Fix this by adding an argument to ovl_get_nlink() that says whether the
caller found an index entry, and by skipping the xattr only if the
caller found none.

Known gaps:
- An index entry that a kernel without this patch left behind for a
  removed file now stays, and the handle of that file keeps working. The
  entry has i_nlink 1 and a stored count of 1, just like the entry of a
  file that was only written by handle. Without this patch, the next
  mount treated it as an orphan.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: fix a torn path in ovl_get_redirect()

A hard link of a metacopy file that races with a rename of an ancestor
stores a redirect to the wrong lower file.

Each component of an absolute redirect must be the name that a dentry
has in the parent that the walk continues with. ovl_get_redirect()
copies the name under d_lock and calls dget_parent() after the unlock,
and the callers for a hard link hold no lock that stops a rename across
directories. A rename between the two steps combines the old name with
the new parent.

With delays in ovl_get_redirect(), an unprivileged user hard-linked a
metacopy file while renaming its ancestor to another directory, the
stored redirect named another lower path, and after a remount the file
showed the data of a root-only file.

Fix this by taking the parent first and checking it again under d_lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: do not copy up an xattr value that was never read

Copy-up stores uninitialized kernel memory in an xattr of the upper
file, where the user can read it.

ovl_copy_xattr() may only pass bytes to ovl_do_setxattr() that
ovl_do_getxattr() has read. When the read fails with -ERANGE the
function asks for the size again, and if the new size fits the buffer
it stores the buffer although nothing was read into it. The buffer
comes from kvmalloc(), or it still holds the value of the previous
xattr.

A FUSE lower layer that answers every sized GETXATTR with -ERANGE made
copy-up store 4096 bytes that the server never sent, with a kernel
pointer in them, as an xattr of the upper file.

Fix this by failing the copy-up with -EIO when the size that follows
-ERANGE fits the buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: do not copy up a dentry that was removed

A change to a removed file through an open descriptor replaces whatever
has its old name in the upper layer.

Copy up must only create a name in the upper directory, never replace
one. After an unlink, an rmdir or a rename over a lower dentry, a
dentry that an open file keeps alive still has its old parent and name,
but in the upper directory that name is now a whiteout or a new object.
ovl_copy_up_workdir() renames the copy over it, which brings back the
removed object and destroys whatever took its name.

An unprivileged user opened a lower FIFO and unlinked it, root created
a file at that name, and fchmod on the old descriptor replaced the file
of root with the FIFO.

Fix this by looking up the target name of the rename in
ovl_copy_up_workdir() with LOOKUP_EXCL, so that copy up fails with
-EEXIST if the name is taken, as copy up with O_TMPFILE already does
when it links the copy to the name.

[amir: use LOOKUP_EXCL instead of relying on d_unhashed()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: check that the parents of volatile/dirty are dirs

An unprivileged user crashes the kernel by mounting overlayfs with the
volatile option.

A dentry that serves as the parent of a lookup must be a directory.
ovl_create_volatile_dirty() walks work/incompat/volatile/dirty by name,
and ovl_lookup_or_create() returns an existing entry whatever its type.
A file or a symlink that another task creates during the mount becomes
the parent of the next lookup, which calls a NULL ->lookup.

An unprivileged user mounted overlayfs with "volatile" in a user
namespace while a second process created a symlink named work/incompat,
and the mount task oopsed on a NULL ->lookup call.

Fix this by returning -ENOTDIR from ovl_lookup_or_create() when the
caller asked for a directory and the existing entry is a non-dir.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: always encode the origin fh when index is enabled

On an overlay with index=on,nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory
crashes the kernel once an LSM has started to deny CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH
to the mounter, the task that mounted the overlay. The mount and the LSM
policy change require root. After that, any user who can write to a
directory that exists only in a lower layer triggers the oops by doing
so.

Before a file or directory that exists only in a lower layer is changed
for the first time, overlayfs copies it to the writable upper layer.
This is called copy up.

On copy up, ovl_get_origin_fh() encodes the file handle of the lower
inode, called the origin. It returns NULL if ovl_can_decode_fh() says
that the lower filesystem cannot decode handles. Whether the callers can
handle NULL depends on the index option:

- Without an index, NULL is fine: the callers store an empty origin
  xattr.
- With index enabled, overlayfs keeps entries for copied up inodes in an
  internal index directory. The name of an index entry is derived from
  the handle, so ovl_get_origin_fh() must return a handle or an error.

The mount only enables the index if ovl_can_decode_fh() succeeds for all
layers, but the result can change later. The function checks the export
operations of the filesystem and capable(CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH). Copy up
runs with the mounter's credentials, and an LSM can start to deny the
capability to those credentials after the mount. ovl_get_origin_fh()
then returns NULL with index enabled.

This goes wrong in two callers:

- With nfs_export=on, copy up of a directory creates an index entry for
  the directory. ovl_create_index() passes the NULL handle to
  ovl_get_index_name_fh(), which dereferences it.
- If the result changes while mount(2) is still running,
  ovl_get_indexdir() passes a NULL from ovl_get_origin_fh() to
  ovl_verify_set_fh() in the same way.

Before the commit in the Fixes tag, these two callers encoded the handle
themselves, without consulting ovl_can_decode_fh().

Reproduced with a BPF LSM program that started to deny the capability
after the mount. An unprivileged touch in a directory that had not been
copied up yet oopsed in ovl_get_index_name_fh(). With this patch the
touch succeeds and the directory gets its index entry.

Fix this by calling ovl_can_decode_fh() in ovl_get_origin_fh() only when
index is disabled.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: use the pinned upper dir in ovl_fix_origin()

Renames made directly on the upper filesystem during a lookup crash the
kernel.

A dentry that is passed to vfs_setxattr() must be pinned.
ovl_fix_origin() passes upper->d_parent to ovl_set_impure() without a
reference, and the lookup holds no lock of the upper directory. A
rename on the upper filesystem changes d_parent, and only the child
pins the new parent, so a second rename and an rmdir free it.

With delays in ovl_fix_origin() and ovl_set_impure(), renaming the upper
directory twice and removing the intermediate parent during the lookup
of a merge directory without an origin xattr gave a KASAN
use-after-free in vfs_setxattr().

Fix this by passing the upper dentry that the overlay parent holds.

[amir: add helper ovl_set_impure_dir()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: take a snapshot of the name for copy up

The copy up of a directory reads a freed dentry name when a lookup
moves the directory at the same time.

A pointer to the name of a dentry is only valid while something stops
a move of the dentry. ovl_do_copy_up() keeps a plain copy of
c->dentry->d_name in c->destname, and ovl_copy_up_start() only keeps
ovl_rename() away. When a lookup finds the same directory under another
name after a change to the lower layer, d_splice_alias() moves the
dentry and frees its external name.

With a delay in ovl_do_copy_up(), a chmod of a lower-only directory with
a 60 byte name raced with a rename of that directory in the lower layer
and a stat of the new name, and KASAN reported a use-after-free in
lookup_noperm_common().

Fix this by using take_dentry_name_snapshot() for c->destname.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: set OVL_WHITEOUTS before publishing the upper dir

Listing a directory while it is copied up causes a use-after-free of
the readdir cache.

A merge directory must never be iterated as a real upper directory:
that mode frees the cache in OVL_I(inode)->cache without looking at
its refcount, while files opened in merged mode still use it.
ovl_copy_up_workdir() publishes the upper dentry before it sets
OVL_WHITEOUTS, and ovl_dir_open() samples both without a lock, so an
open between the two stores finds the upper directory and takes it
for a real one.

With a delay between the two stores, an unprivileged process that
listed a directory during its copy-up saw only "." and "..", and its
next getdents freed the readdir cache of another descriptor.

Fix this by setting OVL_WHITEOUTS before ovl_inode_update(), so that
ovl_dir_reset() agrees with ovl_dir_open(), and by testing
OVL_TYPE_MERGE() of the path type in ovl_dir_open(), so that an open
that observes the upper dentry never iterates a merge dir as a real
dir, regardless of the order in which it observes the flag.

[amir: test OVL_TYPE_MERGE() instead of smp_rmb() in ovl_dir_open()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir

Listing a directory on an overlay uses a freed dentry and crashes the
kernel when a lookup moves the directory at the same time.

Code that can sleep may only use d_parent without a reference while
something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_iterate_real(),
ovl_need_adjust_d_ino() and ovl_cache_update() use the d_parent of the
listed directory and hold only the lock of that directory. When a
lookup finds the directory under another parent after a change to a
layer, d_splice_alias() moves it without that lock and drops its
reference on the old parent.

With a delay in ovl_iterate_real(), getdents64 on an overlay directory
raced a rename in the lower layer and a lookup that moved its dentry,
and after an rmdir of the old parent KASAN reported a use-after-free in
security_inode_getattr().

Fix this by using dget_parent() in the three functions.

[amir: fix comments in ovl_need_adjust_d_ino()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: hold server info until cifsd exits

The last session reference can be dropped while the cifsd demultiplex
thread is still running clean_demultiplex_info(). That thread frees
TCP_Server_Info there, racing with cifs_put_tcp_session() as it releases
the server crypto state. syzbot reported a KASAN use-after-free in
cifs_crypto_secmech_release().

Keep an object reference for the cifsd thread. Defer final crypto,
session-key, network namespace, string, and structure cleanup until both
the last session reference and the thread reference are dropped. Drop the
thread reference after clean_demultiplex_info() has finished using the
server.

Build-tested with ARCH=arm64 and W=1 for
fs/smb/client/connect.o. The KASAN reproducer was not run on the patched
kernel.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix OOB last_entry pointer from unbounded LastNameOffset

CIFSFindFirst() and CIFSFindNext() locate the last entry of a
TRANS2_FIND_FIRST2 or TRANS2_FIND_NEXT2 response by adding the
LastNameOffset of the response parameters to the start of the data
area, and store the result in psrch_inf->last_entry. MS-CIFS 2.2.6.2.2
defines that offset as the offset of the entry's file name; the client
follows the reading of NT and Samba servers, which point it at the
entry. LastNameOffset is only checked against CIFSMaxBufSize, which
says nothing about the response actually received: validate_t2() lets
the data area start up to 1024 bytes into the buffer, and SendReceive()
copies at most CIFSMaxBufSize + MAX_CIFS_HDR_SIZE bytes of a response,
16468 by default, into a cifs_request allocation of CIFSMaxBufSize +
MAX_SMB2_HDR_SIZE bytes, 16588 by default. The pointer itself can
therefore be placed anywhere from the end of the received data to 820
bytes past the end of the allocation.

The read through that pointer is far larger than its displacement.
find_cifs_entry() hands last_entry to cifs_save_resume_key() after every
FindNext and after the FindFirst of a search rewind, and
cifs_fill_dirent() takes the length of the name from the entry itself: a
__le32 FileNameLength for most levels, a __u8 for
SMB_FIND_FILE_INFO_STANDARD, and for SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the result of a
scan for the terminating NUL over up to PATH_MAX + 1 UTF-16 units. The
name is recorded as the resume name of the search, and the next
CIFSFindNext() rejects only a recorded length of PATH_MAX or more before
copying the name into the ResumeFileName of its request and sending it
with the resume key taken from the same entry: up to 4 KiB of memory
from past the end of the allocation leaks to the server, and for
SMB_FIND_FILE_UNIX the NUL scan runs about twice as far before the
length is even known. The entry does not have to lie outside the
response for that either: a maximal response ends about 120 bytes before
the end of the allocation, so an entry in its last bytes with a name
just under PATH_MAX has nearly all of that name copied from past the
allocation.

It needs nothing unusual from the client: a FindNext response that
reports no entries and does not end the search makes find_cifs_entry()
send the next FindNext at once, carrying whatever was parsed at
LastNameOffset, and a search rewind can do the same after its
FindFirst. SMB1 is not negotiated by default: this takes a malicious
or compromised server, a mount of it with an explicit vers=1.0, which

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: snapshot dentry names in file and setattr traces

Patch series "ocfs2: stabilize dentry names in file and setattr traces",
v4.

Snapshot names at all six users of ocfs2__file_ops and at the separate
setattr event. Patch 1 handles the five ordinary file-operation callers
and setattr. Patch 2 handles release separately to preserve its locked
open-count sample and take the snapshot outside that critical section.

The release explanation distinguishes its existing RCU lifetime coverage
from name/length consistency. It does not claim that the ordinary
callers' external-name UAF interleaving crosses the held inode spinlock.
The release source change is unchanged from v3.

Patch 1 also removes the read callback's redundant NULL-inode check.
The two patches apply independently and leave trace formats unchanged.


This patch (of 2):

The open, fsync, read, write and splice-read trace calls pass the live
dentry name and length to the shared ocfs2__file_ops event class.
ocfs2_setattr() passes the same unprotected arguments to its own event.
Both events size and copy a __string field separately. A reference to
the dentry does not pin the external storage backing an individual name.

With an event enabled, a caller can be preempted after loading the name
pointer. A long-to-short rename can then replace the name and reclaim its
old external allocation before the trace callback sizes or copies it,
provided no other snapshot retains that allocation.

The setattr inode lock does not exclude every rename: a same-directory
rename of a source directory need not take that directory's inode lock.
It can therefore change the dentry name while setattr records its event.
Inline names and separately loaded lengths can also change during trace
record sizing and copying.

Take a dentry name snapshot around each of these six trace calls and
pass both the string and length from the snapshot. Check event enablement
before taking a snapshot. Keep the event classes and formats unchanged.

Also remove the redundant NULL-inode check in the read callback.
file_inode() returns the open file's inode, which is already used by the
trace call above the check.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: pin refcount trees before dropping the lookup lock

A refcount tree returned to ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() must stay alive
until that caller releases its operation reference. However,
ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() returns the cached pointer after dropping
osb_lock, and the caller only takes its kref afterwards. The registry
reference does not protect this gap from concurrent removal.

This can happen when another node frees a refcount root and reuses its
block with a different generation while this mount retains the old
cached tree. Two local operations on different inodes sharing the new
root, such as data CoW and an external xattr update, can then look up
the same stale tree. Their inode locks are independent, and both the
REFCOUNT DLM lock and rf_sem are acquired after the first operation
reference.

The following ordering is possible, with no other operation references:

  Data CoW                         Xattr update
  --------                         ------------
  Look up the old tree under
    osb_lock, then drop osb_lock
                                   Look up the same tree and take a kref
                                   Acquire the tree locks and read the
                                     new on-disk generation
                                   Erase the old tree under osb_lock
                                   Unlock and drop the operation kref
                                   Drop the registry kref, freeing tree
  Take a kref through the
    freed tree pointer

The final kref_get() accesses freed rf_getcnt storage, and subsequent
accesses in ocfs2_lock_refcount_tree() also use the freed allocation.

Take the operation reference in ocfs2_get_refcount_tree() before
releasing osb_lock, including when an insertion loses to another lookup.
Removal must acquire the same lock, so it cannot drop the registry
reference before the lookup has pinned the tree. Keep the existing
unlock and error path puts. The two callers that already hold the
refcount tree lock keep their borrowed lookup behavior and do not
acquire an extra reference.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: fix chunk number of the first chunk in a local quota file

Mounting a crafted OCFS2 image can corrupt kernel memory.  When the
local quota file header of such an image claims zero chunks, the first
quota entry allocated during the mount gets a chunk number taken from a
kernel pointer, and releasing that entry clears a bit far outside the
chunk bitmap.

The write will corrupt the data stored at that address, and the
corruption may lead to a system crash or damage unrelated data. 
Mounting requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so it takes an untrusted image, such
as removable media or a loop mount of a file from elsewhere.

Since the chunk number comes from a kernel pointer, the address of the
bit that gets cleared differs from boot to boot, and the issue has been
reported under several titles:

- BUG: unable to handle kernel paging request in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KASAN: slab-use-after-free Write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot
- KFENCE: use-after-free write in ocfs2_local_release_dquot

Note that none of these is a use-after-free in the quota code: the
chunk and its buffer head are alive.  The bit that gets cleared lies
far outside the bitmap.  KASAN and KFENCE name each report based on the
object occupying that address, which explains why the same issue is
reported under so many different titles.  In the report I sent, the
address fell in a free page, which KASAN labels use-after-free.

There are known reproducers.  Both a syzkaller and a C reproducer are
available from the Google Drive link [1] in my report thread.  The
issue was found by our modified syzkaller, not a theoretical thing
found by an LLM.  I have not seen it outside fuzzing, so it is not
affecting me in the real world.

The local quota file in OCFS2 is divided into chunks, and each chunk
begins with a header block holding a bitmap of the quota entries that
chunk has handed out.  Chunks are numbered from zero, and that number is
used to convert the file offset of an entry back into a bit position in
the bitmap.  ocfs2_local_quota_add_chunk() appends a new chunk to the
in-memory list and numbers it one past the chunk that was last:

	list_add_tail(&chunk->qc_chunk, &oinfo->dqi_chunk);
	chunk->qc_num = list_entry(chunk->qc_chunk.prev,
				   struct ocfs2_quota_chunk,
				   qc_chunk)->qc_num + 1;

The predecessor is looked up after the new chunk is added to the list, so
if the list was empty, the prev pointer is the list head itself.  The head
is the dqi_chunk member of struct ocfs2_mem_dqinfo and is not a chunk, so
reading qc_num through it lands 16 bytes past the start of the head, on
the dqi_gqinode pointer that follows it.  The first chunk of the file is
then numbered with the lower half of a kernel pointer instead of 0.

The list is empty when the local quota file header claims the file has no
chunks.  ocfs2_local_read_info() takes dqi_chunks from that header without
validating it, so an image with dqi_chunks == 0 takes this path when the
first quota entry is allocated.

ocfs2_create_local_dquot() turns the bad number into a file offset with
ol_dqblk_off(), which shifts a 32-bit block number left by the block size
bits, so the top bits of such a large block number are lost. 
ocfs2_local_release_dquot() turns the offset back into a bit index with
ol_dqblk_chunk_off(), using the full chunk number, so the lost bits push
that index far outside the bitmap, and clearing it corrupts unrelated
memory.

Compute the chunk number before putting the chunk on the list, and use 0
when the list is empty.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2: cancel quota sync work before freeing quota info

OCFS2 quota info owns dqi_sync_work and must outlive both its timer and
qsync_work_fn().  ocfs2_local_free_info() frees that owner without
cancelling the work, relying on the quota suspend/disable wrappers.

Loading quotas on a read-only to read-write remount can successfully queue
the work in ocfs2_global_read_info() and then fail while attaching a dquot
to an existing inode in add_dquot_ref().  The quota core unwinds that
failure directly through dquot_disable(), bypassing the OCFS2 wrapper:

  Remount task (s_umount write)        Timer/workqueue
  ocfs2_global_read_info()
    schedules dqi_sync_work
  add_dquot_ref() returns an error
  dquot_disable()
    ocfs2_local_free_info()
      frees oinfo
                                     delayed-work timer expires
                                     qsync_work_fn() reads oinfo

The timer core can then write to the freed embedded timer, or
qsync_work_fn() can read oinfo->dqi_gqinode before its s_umount trylock.
The outer ocfs2_disable_quotas() cleanup skips the failed type because
dquot_disable() has already cleared its loaded state.

Cancel dqi_sync_work synchronously at the start of
ocfs2_local_free_info(), before dropping the global inode or freeing any
owner state. The work is initialized whenever read_file_info() succeeds.
dquot_disable() holds s_umount for write, so the callback skips its quota
scan via down_read_trylock() and can finish without waiting for teardown.
The synchronous cancel also handles its self-rearm.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: hold the lookup reference across convert AST enqueue

dlm_convert_lock_handler() drops the reference it took when it found the
lock on res->granted at its leave label, one statement before it calls
dlm_queue_ast().  dlm_free_dead_locks() takes res->spinlock and drops the
list and base references, so a peer death landing in that gap leaves the
handler's own put as the one that frees the lock, and __dlm_queue_ast()
then reads lock->lockres from freed memory.

The handler is registered next to dlm_create_lock_handler(), so a convert
message buffered on a dying peer's socket arrives on the same o2net
receive work that o2net_disconnect_node() does not wait for.  The two can
interleave as follows, with the reference counts as they are before this
fix:

  Socket data-ready       Node-down thread      Receive worker
  -----------------       ----------------      --------------
  o2net_data_ready()
    select sc under
    callback read lock
                          o2net_disconnect_node()
                            queue shutdown
                            begin flush; new color
    queue sc_rx_work
    in the new color
    release callback lock
                            shutdown socket
                            flush returns
                                                read buffered convert_lock
                                                dlm_convert_lock_handler()
                                                  find lock on res->granted
                                                  dlm_lock_get()  refs = 3
                                                  lock res->spinlock
                                                  __dlmconvert_master()
                                                    call_ast = 1
                                                  unlock res->spinlock
                          DLM node-down cleanup
                            lock res->spinlock
                            dlm_free_dead_locks()
                              unlink lock
                              put list ref  refs = 2
                              put base ref  refs = 1
                            unlock res->spinlock
                                                dlm_lock_put()  refs = 0
                                                  free lock
                                                dlm_queue_ast()
                                                  __dlm_queue_ast()
                                                  read lock->lockres
                                                  (use-after-free)

__dlmconvert_master() only moves the lock between lists, so the count
entering the gap is base, list and lookup.  Drop the lookup reference
after the AST is queued instead of before it and the race ends with the
one __dlm_queue_ast() took, which dlm_flush_asts() releases later with
ast_pending cleared and ast_list unlinked.  No extra get is needed, and
the normal case ends with the same count as before.

dlmconvert_master() has the same shape but is only reached from dlmlock()
for a lock this node owns, which dlm_free_dead_locks() never matches.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: hold a lock reference across grant AST enqueue

A newly granted remote lock must remain alive until its grant AST is
queued.  dlmlock_master() publishes the lock on res->granted with its base
and queue references, then drops res->spinlock before calling
dlm_queue_ast().  The resource's reserved AST count does not retain the
lock itself.

This can fail when a peer dies with an immediately grantable CREATE
buffered on its socket.  O2NET's node-down callback flushes receive work
before DLM cleanup, but the flush only waits for work queued on entry.  A
data-ready callback that already selected the socket container can queue
new receive work after the flush advances its work color.  Socket shutdown
does not discard bytes already queued for TCP receive.

The late receive work and DLM node-down cleanup can interleave as
follows (the lock reference operations shown are before this fix):

  Socket data-ready        Node-down thread         Receive worker
  -----------------        ----------------         --------------
  o2net_data_ready()
    select sc under
    callback read lock
                           o2net_disconnect_node()
                             queue shutdown
                             begin flush; new color
    queue sc_rx_work
    in the new color
    release callback lock
                             shutdown socket
                             flush returns
                                                    read buffered CREATE
                                                    dlmlock_master()
                                                      lock res->spinlock
                                                      add lock to granted
                                                      unlock res->spinlock
                           DLM node-down cleanup
                             lock res->spinlock
                             dlm_free_dead_locks()
                               unlink lock
                               put queue/base refs
                               free lock
                             unlock res->spinlock
                                                    dlm_queue_ast()
                                                      __dlm_queue_ast()
                                                      read lock->lockres
                                                      (use-after-free)

DLM cleanup holds res->spinlock while dlm_free_dead_locks() drops the
queue and base references.  The CREATE handler no longer holds that
spinlock when __dlm_queue_ast() reads the lock, before taking its AST list
reference.

Take a temporary lock reference under res->spinlock when a grant AST will
be queued, and drop it after dlm_queue_ast().  This keeps the lock alive
across cleanup until the AST path has taken its own reference, without
reversing the existing AST/resource lock order.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/heartbeat: unlink live slots when their node is missing

o2hb_shutdown_slot() returns immediately when its node is no longer in the
configfs registry.  A slot can still be linked in o2hb_live_slots when
that lookup fails.  Region teardown or startup-error cleanup then frees
the slot array without removing its embedded list member.

With the same peer live in another region, the next list update can follow
a predecessor into the freed array.  Reusing the node number can also make
a later insertion encounter that stale member.

Always remove the slot under o2hb_live_lock, even when node lookup fails. 
Preserve aggregate membership accounting and the last-region DOWN
callback: the existing callback interface explicitly permits a NULL node
for DOWN events.  Only drop the node reference when lookup returned one. 
This closes both normal release and startup-abort paths without changing
the publication or callback locking protocol.

Also require a configured node before admitting a new live slot in
o2hb_check_slot().  The early live-bitmap check is not held through
admission: the last live slot in another region can be removed in between.
Without a node, admission can then queue an UP event with a NULL argument
and hit the event helper's BUG_ON.  Existing live slots can still leave
and generate NULL-node DOWN events.

two regions after removing the peer from configfs.  Its KASAN report

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: Fix use after free in bpf progs

Since commit dccc0c3ddf8f ("media: rc: fix race between unregister and
urb/irq callbacks"), rcdev->raw is no longer set to NULL after device
unregister. raw->progs could point to stale data.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: After rc_unregister_device() timers can be re-armed

If rc_keydown() is called after rc_register_device(), then the timers
can be re-armed. Delete them again for a final time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: Use after free in ir_raw_event_handle()

If rc_unregister_device() is called while IR is being processed, then
ir_raw_event_handle() could call wake_up_process(dev->raw->thread)
after kthread_stop(dev->raw->thread). Avoid use after free by using
get_task_struct().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: mce_kbd: Fix inconsistent locking of keylock

data->keylock is taken with spin_lock() in ir_mce_kbd_decode(), which
runs in the raw IR decode kthread with local interrupts enabled, but
with spin_lock_irqsave() in mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the rx_timeout timer
callback, which runs in softirq context.

If the decode kthread is holding keylock via spin_lock() when a timer
interrupt fires on the same CPU and the softirq runs
mce_kbd_rx_timeout(), the softirq spins forever waiting for a lock
that only the now-preempted kthread can release, while the kthread
cannot run again until the softirq gives up the CPU. This deadlocks
the CPU.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

media: rc: Ensure registered is cleared in error path

If rc_register_device() fails, ensure that registered is not set to true.
If lirc_register() succeeded, then userspace could have an open file
descriptor open. This leads to a use-after-free.

lirc_unregister() must be called with registered = false, else there is a
possibility that an fd is open and polling, which would never return
POLLERR unless registered is false.

Note that registered must be changed under dev->lock, many functions
read registered under lock (e.g. lirc_ioctl).
